talks.title: Strengthening Supply Chain Security: A DevSecOps Perspective by Ankit Giri
talks.teaser: Strengthening Supply Chain Security: A DevSecOps Perspective by Ankit Giri.
talks.summary:
Overview: Ankit Giri of BreachLock presents at CarolinaCon on supply chain security from a DevSecOps perspective, covering risks, challenges, and solutions across the software development lifecycle.

Key Topics: Integrating security into CI/CD pipelines; Infrastructure-as-Code security gaps; AI/ML development tool risks; container and dependency scanning; and building developer-friendly security processes.

Technical Details: Giri warns that IaC templates consumed without security review propagate misconfigurations across entire infrastructures. He discusses how AI-powered development tools introduce new attack surfaces requiring updated security processes.

Takeaways: Supply chain security requires securing code before it becomes infrastructure. DevSecOps teams must address IaC, dependencies, and AI-assisted development as interconnected risk vectors.

talks.title: Repercussions from the Absence of Threat Actor Taxonomy by Jeffrey Bell
talks.teaser: Repercussions from the Absence of Threat Actor Taxonomy by Jeffrey Bell.
talks.summary:
The Naming Problem

Jeffrey Bell argues inconsistent threat-actor naming undermines IOC accumulation and ATT&CK mapping. Without uniform taxonomy, the same actor appears under many aliases—he cites Kim Suuki referenced sixteen different ways across industry reports—fragmenting intelligence sharing.

Threat Actor Categories

Bell groups actors into criminal (financial motives, e.g., Scattered Spider casino breaches), state-sponsored (geopolitical targets including elections, ICS, and research), and hacktivist (ideological, e.g., SiegedSec actions against Heritage Foundation). Overlaps exist, but buckets clarify motive and targeting context.

MITRE ATT&CK as a Shared Language

Using a fictional SOC scenario, he shows vendors like CrowdStrike and Unit 42 independently observing overlapping infrastructure yet struggling to merge attribution. Bell proposes MITRE ATT&CK’s open knowledge base as a neutral framework to align TTPs across naming schemes, improving collective defense without marketing-driven alias proliferation.

talks.title: Explosive overflow: Lessons from rocket science by Mark El-Khoury
talks.teaser: Explosive overflow: Lessons from rocket science by Mark El-Khoury.
talks.summary:
From Pentest PDFs to Systems Thinking

Mark El-Khoury recounts moving from repetitive penetration testing (“bug-to-PDF factory”) to product security engineering, inspired by Kelly Shortridge’s view that security is a subset of system resilience—not isolated component checks.

Ariane 5 and Integer Overflow

The Ariane 5 maiden flight exploded 30 seconds after launch when a 64-bit inertial velocity value converted to 16-bit overflowed, crashing guidance software—a famous case of reused Ariane 4 assumptions without range analysis despite static analysis tooling available pre-launch.

Secure Development Reality

Effective programs pair static analysis, dependency review, IaC scanning, secret removal, threat modeling, and training with engineering-friendly culture: low friction, psychological safety, and avoiding reflexive “no” that teams ignore. White House cyber policy highlights hardware, formal methods, and memory-safe languages—each costly at scale (e.g., rewriting massive C++ game engines impractical).

Google and Industry Memory Safety

Google’s advancing memory safety paper acknowledges gradual Rust adoption plus hardening C/C++ because full rewrites are unrealistic. Formal verification (Amazon s2n-TLS) works but demands enormous specialized effort; Ken Thompson’s trusting-trust essay reminds limits of any single assurance layer.

talks.title: "Ok I guess we doin' shells now:" Creating a Secure Web Server from Two Vulnerable Web Servers
talks.teaser: "Ok I guess we doin' shells now:" Creating a Secure Web Server from Two Vulnerable Web Servers.
talks.summary:
Consensus-based defense

The speaker proposes building a secure web front end from two different vulnerable servers using Shell HTTP Response Factory logic: instead of detecting exploits after compromise, compare normalized HTTP responses from both backends on each request. If at least one stack is secure for a given flaw, mismatched output blocks the attack.

Normalization challenges

Responses must be made comparable by stripping or harmonizing server headers, cookies, JavaScript dictionary ordering, and similar differences before equality checks. The proxy needs no exploit-specific signatures or historical baseline—only live agreement between peers.

Historical examples

Code Red's IIS buffer overflow would diverge from a Linux peer. Heartbleed-style memory leaks would not match a properly responding sibling. A CrowdStrike-like host failure can trigger failover to cold spares while preserving consensus guarantees. XZ Utils' liblzma backdoor affected many Linux tools but not Windows lz32.dll, so heterogeneous pairs reduce supply-chain single-point risk.

Use cases

The approach suits legacy binaries, mixed-platform stacks, and deliberate risk diversification when one component is known vulnerable.
